title: EvalStructure: Minimal Abstraction of a CCC
content: EvalStructure axiomatizes exactly the data needed for Lawvere's theorem: an object type Ob (codes/programs), a value type Val (outputs), and an evaluation eval : Ob → Ob → Val (applying a code to an input). This corresponds to the key morphism ev ∘ ⟨e, id⟩ : A → B in a CCC. IsPointSurjective captures the condition that e : A → B^A is a 'point-surjection': every function Ob → Val is represented by some code.
mathContext: $\text{EvalStructure} = (\text{Ob}, \text{Val}, \text{eval} : \text{Ob} \to \text{Ob} \to \text{Val})$. IsPointSurjective: $\forall g : \text{Ob} \to \text{Val},\; \exists a_0 \in \text{Ob},\; \forall x,\; \text{eval}(a_0, x) = g(x)$. Corresponds to $e : A \to B^A$ surjective on global elements $1 \to B^A$.

title: lawvere_abstract: The Diagonal in 2 Lines
content: The proof of the abstract Lawvere FPT is remarkably short: construct the diagonal function g(a) = f(eval(a, a)), use point-surjectivity to find a₀ with eval(a₀, x) = g(x) for all x, then evaluate at a₀ to get eval(a₀, a₀) = g(a₀) = f(eval(a₀, a₀)) — so eval(a₀, a₀) is a fixed point of f. This is the distilled form of all diagonal arguments: one variable is the 'code', the other is the 'input', and the diagonal makes them the same.
mathContext: Let $g(a) = f(\text{eval}(a,a))$. Point-surjectivity: $\exists a_0,\; \forall x,\; \text{eval}(a_0,x) = g(x)$. At $x = a_0$: $\text{eval}(a_0,a_0) = g(a_0) = f(\text{eval}(a_0,a_0))$. So $v = \text{eval}(a_0,a_0)$ satisfies $f(v) = v$.

title: diagonal_not_representable: Cantor's Argument Made Explicit
content: The explicit contrapositive: the diagonal function g(a) = f(eval(a, a)) is never representable by any code when f has no fixed point. If a₀ represented g, then eval(a₀, a₀) = f(eval(a₀, a₀)), giving a fixed point — contradicting f being fixed-point-free. This is exactly Cantor's original argument: the 'anti-diagonal' function can't be in any enumeration.
mathContext: If $\exists a_0,\; \forall x,\; \text{eval}(a_0,x) = f(\text{eval}(x,x))$, then at $x = a_0$: $\text{eval}(a_0,a_0) = f(\text{eval}(a_0,a_0))$, so $f$ has a fixed point. Contrapositive: fixed-point-free $f$ $\Rightarrow$ diagonal not representable.

title: Type-Theoretic Recovery: EvalStructure from e : A → A → B
content: typeEvalStructure builds an EvalStructure from any function e : A → A → B by setting Ob = A, Val = B, eval = e. The surjectivity equivalence shows that IsPointSurjective for this structure is exactly Function.Surjective e (Lean's standard surjectivity). This reduces the abstract theorem to the type-theoretic version: lawvere_type_recovery = one line calling lawvere_abstract on the typeEvalStructure.
mathContext: $\text{typeEvalStructure}(A, B, e) = (A, B, e)$. $\text{IsPointSurjective} \iff \text{Function.Surjective}(e)$ (via funext). lawvere_type_recovery: $\text{Surjective}(e) \Rightarrow \forall f : B \to B,\; \exists b,\; f(b) = b$.

title: Three Concrete Instances: Prop, Bool, ℕ
content: Three instances of the abstract theorem: (1) Cantor instance: Val = Prop, f = Not — No e : A → A → Prop can be point-surjective, because Not has no fixed point (¬P = P is impossible). (2) Bool instance: Val = Bool, f = (!·) — Similarly. (3) Nat_succ instance: Val = ℕ, f = Nat.succ — Since n+1 ≠ n, no evaluation on ℕ can be point-surjective. Each proof is just 3-5 lines applying lawvere_abstract and deriving the contradiction.
mathContext: Cantor: $\neg P = P$ impossible. Bool: $!b = b$ impossible ($! \text{false} = \text{true} \neq \text{false}$). ℕ: $n + 1 = n$ impossible. All three follow from lawvere_abstract + the impossibility of a fixed point.

title: CategoricalEval and lawvere_categorical: Global Elements in a CCC
content: CategoricalEval axiomatizes more of the CCC structure: objects Obj, morphisms Hom, exponential objects exp, global elements Pt (morphisms from the terminal object), evaluation apply : Pt(B^A) → Pt(A) → Pt(B), and point-surjectivity ptSurj. The theorem lawvere_categorical takes an explicit e_pt : Pt A → Pt(exp A B) (the morphism's Yoneda action on global elements) and reduces the proof to lawvere_abstract via an EvalStructure with eval a x = apply (e_pt a) x. The entire proof is one term-mode line.
mathContext: CCC data: $\text{Pt}(A)$ = global elements $1 \to A$. Evaluation: $\text{apply} : \text{Pt}(B^A) \to \text{Pt}(A) \to \text{Pt}(B)$. EvalStructure: $\text{Ob} = \text{Pt}(A)$, $\text{Val} = \text{Pt}(B)$, $\text{eval}(a, x) = \text{apply}(e_{\text{pt}}(a), x)$.

title: Topos Connection and Proxy Cantor
content: In a topos, Cantor's theorem states no object surjects onto its power object P(A) = Ω^A, where Ω is the subobject classifier. With f = ¬ (internal negation on Ω), f has no fixed point (¬⊤ = ⊥ ≠ ⊤), so Lawvere prevents any surjection A → Ω^A. topos_proxy_cantor uses Prop as a proxy for Ω, recovering Cantor's theorem in the type-theoretic setting. The full topos formalization requires Mathlib's topos infrastructure.
mathContext:
Topos Cantor: $\Omega$ has negation $
eg : \Omega 	o \Omega$ with no fixed point ($
eg 	op =  ot 
eq 	op$). Lawvere: no $e : A 	o \Omega^A$ is point-surjective. Proxy: $\Omega = 	ext{Prop}$, recovering $
eg \exists e : A 	o A 	o 	ext{Prop},\; 	ext{Surjective}(e)$.
